# Oakwood Cemetery

## Established 1879

## Fort Worth’s Historic Cemetery

#### “Simple paths dappled with shade from giant oaks and a casual stroll from the past toward today.”

— John Peter Smith, Fort Worth Pioneer

Overlooking the Trinity River and dotted with beautiful oak trees, Oakwood Cemetery offers an impressive view of downtown Fort Worth. Oakwood is the resting place of an eclectic mix of Texas and Fort Worth legends: founding families, cattle barons, mayors, gamblers and gunslingers, educators, confederate soldiers, and bartender and bricklayer union members.

The cemetery was designated a Texas historical site in 1966 and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2018.

---

Oakwood Cemetery is a non-profit, registered Texas Historic cemetery in Fort Worth, TX.

And as a 501c13 non-profit organization all donations are tax deductible and go to the maintenance and improvement of one of Fort Worth’s most beautiful and historic places. Your generosity makes all the difference. Please give and support the cemetery’s care and maintenance today.

—John Peter SmithFort Worth Pioneer

# Paths in History

Oakwood is a living part of historic Fort Worth. Its rustic paths meander through memories with the names and stories of the earliest founders side by side with those of later generations and through today.

Upon the death of his stepson Frank L. Fox, Fort Worth pioneer John Peter Smith donated 20 acres for the cemetery on December 26, 1879. The burial is believed to be the oldest in what was then simply called New Cemetery.

As more and more citizens followed their friends and family across the Trinity to this peaceful spot, the cemetery grew to more than 60 acres in three connected sections and became known as Oakwood. Oakwood is the second oldest cemetery in Fort Worth and was known as "City Cemetery" or "New City Cemetery" until it was renamed "Oakwood" in 1885. An estimated 350 graves were moved from White Settlement Cemetery to Oakwood between 1952 and 1953 to make room for the Carswell Air Force Base runway extension. Many of these graves are unmarked.

In 1912 the Oakwood Cemetery Chapel was erected and now, fully renovated, stands proudly at the entry.

The cemetery has grown to over 100 acres and contains two additional distinct areas: Old Trinity and Calvary.

## Calvary Cemetery

Calvary, situated on the southeast edge of Oakwood, was partitioned for the Catholic Church.

This three-acre cemetery was established in 1880 when John Peter Smith donated the parcel to the Bishop of Galveston for use as a Catholic cemetery. The rectangular tract is partially bordered on the north by Soldiers Row and is immediately south of City Cemetery. Entrance to the cemetery is from the west. It is marked by a gate that straddles the main drive.

Erected in 1922, it has a wrought iron arch containing the words “Calvary Cemetery.” The arch is supported by square brick columns.

## City Cemetery

What was originally known as City Cemetery is the city’s second oldest cemetery. Created in 1879, the publicly-owned City Cemetery was composed of seventeen acres and was donatd by John Peter Smith. It has a rectangular plan consisting of four rows with four blocks each. The blocks are number 1 through 16.

By the late 1890s, City Cemetery had been expanded to the west and south. These privately-owned areas were known as East and West Oakwood. By the late 1890s, the City Cemetery and East and West Oakwood collectively became known as Oakwood. Today, all of the cemeteries are under the management of the Oakwood Cemetery Association.

## Old Trinity Cemetery

Old Trinity Cemetery , located on the northern edge of Oakwood, was the designated cemetery for the burials of African Americans.

Old Trinity is the final resting place for many Tarrant County citizens of African American decent. One of those buried there is William Madison "Gooseneck" McDonald who was a successful businessman and active in politics. The McDonald monument, the tallest in the cemetery, was erected by "Gooseneck" on his family plot. He arranged for beautiful granite slabs to be placed on the graves of family that preceded him in death, but his grave remains unmarked.
